Conferring jurisdiction

Arrest, when valid, vests jurisdiction to the court over

the person of the accused. To emphasize, it is the arrest

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

of the person and not the issuance of a warrant of

arrest.

It is the valid arrest of the person or the voluntary

submission or appearance in court, which vests

jurisdiction over the person of the accused. It is not the

issuance of the warrant of arrest.

Description of the person

 Section 2 of Article III, 1987

Constitution

 The issuance of a general warrant or a

warrant which do not particularly

describe or particularly name the

person to be seized or even the

issuance of a warrant to several persons

who cannot be identified is clearly a

violation of the Constitution.

 if a person subject of a warrant of arrest

is only identified by his nickname or by

an appellation by which he is known,

he must be described in the warrant of

arrest with particularity, such that the

person who will effect the arrest using

the warrant of arrest may be able to

zero in or identify the person of the

accused or the person to be arrested.

Section 3. Duty of arresting officer. — It shall be the

duty of the officer executing the warrant to arrest the

accused and to deliver him to the nearest police

station or jail without unnecessary delay.

Section 4. Execution of warrant. — The head of the

office to whom the warrant of arrest was delivered

for execution shall cause the warrant to be executed

within ten (10) days from its receipt. Within ten

(10) days after the expiration of the period, the

officer to whom it was assigned for execution shall

make a report to the judge who issued the warrant.

In case of his failure to execute the warrant, he shall

state the reasons therefor.

Lifetime of the warrant of arrest

It shall remain valid and effective so long as it has not

been recalled or the person named therein has not been

arrested or has not submitted himself to the

jurisdiction of the court. The validity of the warrant

continues even if the officer assigned to execute has

made a negative return to the issuing court.

Section 4, on the execution of warrant, the timeframes

there are only to ensure that there is dispatch in the

execution of the warrant of arrest. If there is failure to

execute the warrant of arrest then based on Section 4,

the person or the enforcement officer assigned to

execute the warrant shall only make a report to the

judge who made or issued the warrant. In case there is

failure to execute the warrant, he is duty bound to state

the reasons therefore.

GR: warrant of arrest does not expire

XPN: it is recalled or there is a voluntary submission

of the person to be arrested to the jurisdiction of the

court.

Duties of the arresting officer (People v. Mahinay)

At the time a person is arrested it shall be the duty of

the arresting officer

1) The person arrested, detained, invited or under

custodial investigation must be informed in a

language known to and understood by him of

the reason for the arrest, and he must be shown

the warrant of arrest if any, every other

warnings information or communication must

be in a language known to and understood by

said person.

Take note, however, that under the last

sentence of Section 7 of Rule 113, the officer

need not have the warrant in his possession at

the time of the arrest, but after the arrest if the

person arrested so requires the warrant shall be

shown to him as soon as practicable.

Under the first guideline, if the arresting officer

has in his custody the warrant of arrest then,

when the arresting officer explains to the

person being arrested the reason for his

arrest, he can already show the warrant of

arrest. But if, for example, it is not in his

custody as of the moment of the arrest then,

Section 7 of Rule 113 will apply.

2) He must be warned that he has the right to

remain silent, and that any statement he makes

may be used as evidence against him.

3) He must be informed that he has the right to

be assisted at all times and have the presence of

an

independent

and

competent

lawyer

preferably of his own choice.

4) He must be informed that if he has no lawyer

or cannot afford the services of a lawyer, one

will be provided for him, and that a lawyer may

also be engaged by any person in his behalf, or

may be appointed by the court upon petition

of the person arrested, or one acting in his

behalf.

5) That whether or not the person arrested has a

lawyer, he must be informed that no custodial

investigation in any form shall be conducted

except in the presence of his counsel, or after a

valid waiver has been made. Take note that the

waiver of the right to be represented by counsel

must be in writing and must be signed in the

presence of counsel.

6) The person arrested must be informed that at

any time he has a right to communicate or

confer by the most expedient means -

telephone, radio, letter or messenger - with his

lawyer, either retained or appointed, any

member of his immediate family, or any

medical doctor, priest or minister chosen by

him or by anyone from his immediate family or

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

by his counsel, or be visited by, or confer with

duly accredited national or international non-

government organization. It shall be the

responsibility of the officer to ensure that this

is accomplished.

7) He must be informed that he has the right to

waive any of the said rights provided it is made

voluntarily, knowingly, and intelligently and

ensure that he understood the same.

8) In addition, if the person arrested waives his

right to a lawyer, he must be informed that it

must be done in writing and in the presence of

counsel, otherwise, he must be warned that the

waiver is void even if he insists on his waiver

and chooses to speak.

9) The person arrested must be informed that he

may indicate in any manner at any time or stage

of the process that he does not wish to be

questioned with warning, that once he makes

such indication that indication, the police may

not interrogate him if the same had not yet

commenced, or the interrogation must cease if

it has already begun.

10) The person arrested must be informed that his

initial waiver of his right to remain silent, the

right to counsel or any of his rights does not

bar him from invoking it at any time during the

process, regardless of whether he may have

answered some questions or volunteered some

statements.

11) He must also be informed that any statement

or evidence, as the case may be, obtained in

violation of any of the foregoing, whether

inculpatory or exculpatory, in whole or in part,

shall be inadmissible in evidence.

It is not enough for the person arresting to merely

repeat to the person under investigation the provisions

of Section 12, Art. 3 of the 1987 Constitution. The

former must also explain the effects of such provision

in practical terms.

Art. 125. Delay in the delivery of detained persons

to the proper judicial authorities. – The penalties

provided in the next preceding article shall be

imposed upon the public officer or employee who

shall detain any person for some legal ground and

shall fail to deliver such person to the proper judicial

authorities within the period of: twelve (12) hours,

for crimes or offenses punishable by light penalties,

or their equivalent; eighteen (18) hours, for crimes

or offenses punishable by correctional penalties, or

their equivalent; and thirty-six (36) hours, for crimes

or offenses punishable by afflictive or capital

penalties, or their equivalent.

Section 5. Arrest without warrant; when lawful. — A

peace officer or a private person may, without a

warrant, arrest a person:

(a) When, in his presence, the person to be arrested

has committed, is actually committing, or is

attempting to commit an offense; [what is otherwise

known as in flagrante delicto arrest]

(b) When an offense has just been committed, and

he has probable cause to believe based on personal

knowledge of facts or circumstances that the person

to be arrested has committed it; [otherwise known

as "hot pursuit arrest"] and

(c) When the person to be arrested is a prisoner who

has escaped from a penal establishment or place

where he is serving final judgment or is temporarily

confined while his case is pending, or has escaped

while being transferred from one confinement to

another. In cases falling under paragraph (a) and (b)

above, the person arrested without a warrant shall be

forthwith delivered to the nearest police station or

jail and shall be proceeded against in accordance

with Section 7 of Rule 112. (5a)

Warrantless arrests

Warrantless arrest is a seizure of person without a

warrant but based on probable cause that he has

committed a felony or has escaped from confinement.

"to hold that no criminal can, in any case, be arrested

and searched for the evidence and tokens of his

crime without a warrant, would be to leave society,

to a large extent, at the mercy of the shrewdest, the

most expert, and the most depraved of criminals,

facilitating their escape in many instances. (Umil v.

Ramos)

IN FLAGRANTE DELICTO

A peace officer or private person may, without a

warrant, arrest a person when

1) in his presence, the person to be arrested has

committed, is actually committing, or is

attempting to commit an offense

2) The arresting officer therefore must have

personal knowledge of such fact or personal

knowledge

of

facts

and

circumstances

convincingly indicative or constitutive of

probable cause.

Elements

1) The person to be arrested must execute an

overt act indicating that he has just committed,

is actually committing, or is attempting to

commit a crime; and

2) Such overt act is done in the presence or

within the view of the arresting officer or

private person

 It must be stressed that the presence

not only requires that the arresting

person sees the offense, but also when

he hears the disturbance created

thereby and proceeds at once to the

scene.

An arrest made after an entrapment operation

does not require a warrant in as much as it is

considered as a valid warrantless arrest. Considering

that an arrest was lawfully made, the search

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

incidental to such arrest was also valid (People v.

Collado)

It should be stressed that the Supreme Court has

already ruled that a buy-bust operation is a form of

entrapment which has repeatedly been accepted to

be a valid means of arresting violators of the

Dangerous Drugs Law.

The justification that underlies the legitimacy of the

buy-bust operation is that the suspect is arrested in

flagrante delicto – that is the suspect has just

committed or is in the act of committing or is

attempting to commit the offense in the presence of

the arresting police officer or private person.

The arresting police officer or private person is

favored in such an instance with a presumption of

regularity in the performance of official duties

(People v. Andaya)

When the accused was arrested while merely talking

to a police informant, and there was no overt act

indicative of a felonious enterprise that could be

properly attributed to the said accused to arouse

suspicion in the mind of the arresting officer that the

accused

has

just

committed,

was

actually

committing, or was attempting to commit a crime,

the warrantless arrest was not valid.

As testified to by the arresting officer himself in the

same case, the accused and the informant were just

talking to each other and there was no exchange of

money and drugs when he approached the car. He

also admitted on cross-examination that he had no

personal knowledge on whether there was a

prohibited drug and gun inside the vehicle of the

accused when he approached (People v. Edaño)

The police claims that they were alerted when they

saw two unidentified men suddenly rush out of a

house and since they suspected that a crime had

been committed, the natural thing for them to do

was to give chase to the jeep that the two fleeing men

boarded given that the officers were in a patrol car

and a tricycle.

Although running after the fleeing suspect was the

more urgent task, the officer instead gave priority to

the house even when they heard no cry for help from

it.

Admittedly, the police officer did not notice

anything amiss going on the house from the street

where they stood. Now, even if they peek through

the partially open door of the house, they saw no

activity that warranted them entering it.

Clearly, no crime was plainly exposed to the view

of the arresting officer that authorize the arrest

of the accused without a warrant. (Antiquera v.

People)

The mere act of darting away when approached by a

police officer should not be construed against the

accused. Flight per se is not synonymous with

guilt and must not always be attributed to one's

consciousness of guilt.

Flight is not a reliable indicator of guilt without other

circumstances. An attempt to run away from an

officer is susceptible to various explanation; it could

signify guilt or may signify innocence. There are

many innocent reasons for flight like fear or

retribution for speaking to an officer, unwillingness

to appear as witness, and fear of being apprehended

even if he is innocent.

Also, the act of walking along the street and holding

something in one's hand, even if they appeared to be

dubious, coupled with his previous criminal charge

for the same offense, are not by themselves

sufficient to insight suspicion of criminal activity, or

to create probable cause enough to justify a

warrantless arrest.

A previous criminal charge for the same offense are

not by themselves sufficient to incite suspicion of

criminal activity or to create probable cause enough

to justify a warrantless arrest. (People v. Villareal)

Running away per se is not a crime and suspicion

that a crime is being committed is not sufficient to

establish probable cause. In In Flagrante Delicto

cases, there should be a crime being committed and

not a mere suspicion that a crime is being

committed.

suspicion that someone is committing a crime is not

the same as having personal knowledge that a crime

is being committed.

The SC rejected the validity of an arrest made by an

officer on the basis of his observation that the

accused was standing around and showing improper

and unpleasant movements. Such acts declared by

the Supreme Court cannot be considered as criminal

acts. At the time, the officer was aboard a

motorcycle cruising at the speed of 30kph when he

allegedly saw the accused while standing on the side

of the street and handing over something to another

at distance of 10m. The Court finds it is implausible

even assuming that he had a perfect vision to have

been able to identify minuscule amounts of

crystalline substances inside two plastic sachets

(Comerciante v. People)

The arrest was made because of a mere tip of an

informant and it became the reason for the

warrantless arrest and the corresponding search that

happened thereafter.

The person arrested here was just descending from

a ship holding a bag and there was no outward

indication that he was committing any crime.

The rule will be for tips of informants is that there

should be probable cause to arrest a person before

he can be validly arrested without warrant and

thereafter searched. There must be an overt act of

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

committing a crime to be the basis of probable cause

in in flagrante delicto cases. (People v. Aminnudin)

The allegations upon which the probable cause was

based was that the person arrested was seen with his

eyes moving fast and looking at every person passing

by. Again, there is no crime being committed by the

person arrested. (Malacat v. CA)

There was a tip from a telephone call to the police

by an alleged informer that there was a suspicious

looking man where at a street corner at Tondo

shortly before noon. The police operatives

dispatched to the place so three men one of whom

turned out to be Mengote who was looking from

side to side clutching his abdomen- these were the

"overt acts".

The Supreme Court ruled that there was nothing

clandestine about him being on the street at the busy

hour in the blaze of the noon day and by no stretch

of imagination is looking from side to side and

clutching his abdomen a criminal act. Thus, there

was no valid warrantless arrest. (People v.

Mengote)

A day before the arrest the officers were informed

that there was a schedule delivery of shabu by

their employer WWW which will be done early in the

morning and that he could be found at a certain

apartment building in Malate, Manila. The police

operatives decided to look for WWW to shed light

for the illegal drug activities alleged by the employees

and proceeded to the location of the apartment and

placed the same under surveillance. When WWW

came out of the apartment towards a parked car, two

other police officers approached him and introduced

themselves to him as police officers, asked his name

and upon hearing that he's WWW immediately

frisked him and asked him to open the back

compartment of the car. When frisked, there was

found inside the front right pocket of WWW an

unlicensed pistol and ammunitions.

At the same time, the other members of the

operatives searched the car and found inside it the ff

items: transparent plastic bags of shabu, Php 650,

000 cash, electronic and mechanical scales and

another unlicensed pistol with magazine.

The Supreme Court said that the facts and

circumstances surrounding the case did not manifest

any suspicious behavior on the part of WWW that

would reasonably invite the attention of the police.

He was merely walking from the apartment and was

about to enter a parked car when the police

operatives arrested him, frisked, and searched his

person and commanded him to open the

compartment of the car. He was not committing any

visible offense then and the SC reiterated that

reliable information alone absent any overt act

indicative of a felonious enterprise in the

presence and within the view of the arresting

officers is not sufficient to constitute probable

cause to justify an in flagrante delicto arrest. The

SC concluded that there can be no valid warrantless

arrest in in flagrante delicto under the facts and

circumstances of the case. (People v. Laguio Jr)

HOT PURSUIT ARREST

A peace officer or private person may, without warrant,

arrest a person when an offense has just been

committed, and he has probable cause to believe, based

on personal knowledge of facts or circumstances that

the person to be arrested has committed it.

Two conditions

1) the person to be arrested must have just

committed an offense; and

2) the arresting peace officer or private person has

probable cause to believe, based on

personal

knowledge

of

facts

or

circumstances that the person to be

arrested is the one who committed the

offense.

In flagrante

Hot pursuit

require that the arresting

officer or private person

to personally witness the

commission

of

the

offence.

does not require that the

arresting

officer

or

private

person

to

personally witness the

commission

of

the

offence. In fact, the

offense

was

not

committed

in

his

presence, although said

offense as required by

their rules has just been

committed.

No

relation

immediacy

There must be a large

measure of immediacy

between the time the

offense was committed

and the time of the

arrest.

Personal knowledge

This personal knowledge must amount to probable

cause, which means actual belief or reasonable grounds

of suspicion. The grounds of suspicion are reasonable

when in the absence of actual belief of the arresting

officers, the suspicion that a person arrested is

probably guilty of committing the offense is based

on actual facts

The person making the arrest has personal knowledge

of the fact that the crime was committed, because at

the time of the arrest, he has a reasonably worthy

information in his possession coupled with his own

observation and fair inferences therefrom, that the

person arrested has probably committed the offense.

The arresting officer may even rely on information

supplied by a witness or a victim of the crime.

Two robbers divested the passenger of a Jeepney of

their belongings, including a jacket of one passenger.

The passengers immediately sought the help of a

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

police officer, which form a team to track down the

suspects. One of the passengers who went with the

responding police officers saw one of the robbers

casually walking in the same vicinity and wearing his

jacket. The warrant of arrest of the accused was

sustained by the court as well within the hot

pursuit exception.

So long as there was a continuous hot pursuit of that

particular person who committed the crime, then it

may be argued that it is still a valid warrantless arrest,

even if it is made days after. (People v. Acol)

The Valenzuela police station received a report of a

mauling incident, which resulted in the death of the

victim who received a massive skull fracture caused

by a hard and heavy object.

The court ruled that, based on their knowledge of

the circumstances of the death of the victim, and

the report of an eyewitness in arresting the

accused, the officers had personal knowledge of

facts leading them to believe that it was the accused

who was one of the perpetrators of the crime.

(People v. Gerente)

The petitioner alleged that he was arrested based

merely on information relayed to the police officers

about a shooting incident and that they had at the

time of the arrest no personal knowledge of the

facts. The court found that as soon as the police

received a phone call about a shooting incident, a

team

was

dispatched

to

investigate.

The

investigation disclosed that a victim was wounded

and that the witnesses tagged the petitioner as the

one involved and that he had just left the scene of

the crime. After tracking down the petitioner, he was

invited to the police headquarters. But the petitioner

who initially agreed, sped off prompting the

authorities to give chase.

The court ruled that the petitioners act of trying to

get away, coupled with the incident report, which

they investigated is enough to raise a reasonable

suspicion on the part of the police authorities to the

existence of probable cause. (Abelita v. Doria)

Petitioner Robin Padilla figured in a hit and run

accident with a Mitsubishi Pajero. The incident was

witnessed by Manarang, a member of a civic group.

Manarang rode this motorcycle and chased the

petitioner. It was able to make out the plate number,

PMA 777. He called the Viper through the radio,

which flashed the message to all units of PNP

Angeles City. PNP mobile patrols responded to the

call and at Abacan Bridge Manarang found mobile

three with SPO 2 Borja and SPO 2 Miranda. He

informed them about the hit and run incident and he

returned to where he came from until he saw the

vehicle that figured in the incident, and he followed

it. Soon the vehicle was within sight of SPO 2 Borja

and Miranda of Mobile No. 3. They rode their

mobile car and cut into the path of the vehicle

forcing it to stop.

The police officer requested petitioner to alight the

vehicle. When he alighted with his hands raised, a

gun tucked in the left of his waist was revealed. The

gun was confiscated and his car was searched for

weapons which turned out to contain firearms and

ammunitions of assorted caliber. Petitioner insisted

that his arrest was illegal, arguing that the arresting

officer were not at the scene of the hit and run.

The SC held that although the policemen who

apprehended petitioner were not at the scene of the

hit and run, such fact did not affect the propriety of

the apprehension. It was in fact the most prudent

action Manarang could have taken rather than

collaring petitioner himself in as much as policemen

are better trained in performing an arrest of suspects

who, in this case is Robin Padilla. Petitioner could

have put up a degree of resistance which an

untrained civilian could not contain without putting

himself in danger.

In that case, there was a valid arrest in hot pursuit

because the witness to the hit and run informed the

police officers of the plate number of the car which

caused the hit and run, thus, the policemen called

went after the said vehicle. When the vehicle was

cornered, Robin Padilla alighted. Therefore, there

were crucial facts and circumstances that would lead

a prudent man to believe that the hit and run was

committed by person driving the vehicle who is

probably guilty of committing the crime. (Padilla v.

CA)

ARREST OF ESCAPED PRISONERS

When the person to be arrested is a prisoner who has

1) escaped from a penal establishment or place

where he is serving final judgment or is

temporarily confined while his case is pending,

or

2) has escaped while being transferred from one

confinement to another

3) An accused who files a fake bail bond is

considered not merely to have jumped bail but

for all intents and purposes, to have escaped

from detention, thus, such accused may be

rearrested without warrant.

Revised Rule of Criminal Procedure

1) An accused released on bail may be re-

arrested without a necessity of a warrant if

he attempts to depart from the Philippines

without permission of the court where the case

is pending.

2) For the purpose of surrendering the accused

the bondsman may arrest him, or upon

written authority endorsed on a certified copy

of the undertaking, cause him to be arrested by

a police officer or any other person of suitable

age and discretion. (Section 23 of rule 114)

3) If a person lawfully arrested escapes or is

rescued, any person may immediately pursue

or take him without a warrant at any time and

in any place within the Philippines (Section 13

Custodial investigation

Under RA No. 7438, the so called invitation of a

person in connection with an offense he is suspected

to have committed is a prohibited act for which the

inviting officer may be held liable under sections 2(f)

and 4 of RA No. 7438.

The mere invitation is already covered by the

prescription on warrantless arrest because it is intended

for no other reason than to conduct a custodial

investigation.

Custodial investigation shall already include the

practice of issuing an invitation to a person who is

investigated in connection with an offense he is

suspected to have committed.

This means even those who voluntarily surrender

before a police officer must be apprised of their

Miranda rights for the same pressures: whether you

were invited or you were arrested or you voluntarily

went there, the same pressures of custodial setting exist

in whatever scenario.

POSSIBLE REMEDIES AGAINST ILLEGAL

ARREST

1) He or any person in his behalf may file a

verified petition for habeas corpus before the

proper court if no complaint or information is

filed against him in court. (Sec 1, 2, 3 Rule 102)

2) He may apply for bail with any court in the

province or city or municipality where he is

held. (Section 17 of Rule 114)

3) He may, if a complaint against him is

commenced before the proper officer for

inquest investigation, ask for a regular

preliminary investigation and raise the issue of

his illegal arrest. Ofcourse after signing the

waiver (Section 7 of Rule 112)

4) He may, if a complaint or information is filed

against him in court for an offense requiring a

preliminary

investigation,

asked

for

a

preliminary investigation within five (5) days

from the time he learns of the filing of the

complaint, or information (Section 7 of Rule

112)

5) He may, before entering his plea, move to

quash the complaint or information on the

ground that the court has no jurisdiction over

his person

The person arrested has the right to question the

illegality of his arrest, whether with the warrant or

without warrant. However, any objection involving

a warrant of arrest or the procedure by which the

court acquires jurisdiction of the person of the

accused, for example, in warrantless arrest; it must

be made before he enters his plea.

When the accused has already entered his plea and

participates during the trial without previously

invoking his objections, then he is deemed to have

waived his right to question the illegality of his arrest.

There is also an instance where a previously illegal

warrantless arrest may be validated by the issuance

of a warrant of arrest

The filing of charges and the issuance of warrant of

arrest against a person invalidly detained will cure the

defect, that the detention or at least deny him the

right to be released because of such defect. the

accused may be arrested by virtue of that warrant of

arrest and therefore, the issue of whether there was

a valid warrantless arrest will become moot and

academic.

Effects of failure to file a timely objection to illegal

warantless arrest

1) only the right to assail their arrest is waived

2) He does not waive the right to question the

admissibility of the evidence seized by virtue of

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

the illegal arrest. Thus, the fruit of the

poisonous tree still applies.

3) Legality of the arrest affects only the

jurisdiction of the court over the person of

the accused. The illegality of the arrest cannot

in itself be the basis for acquittal as it will

not negate the validity of the conviction of the

accused.

4) even if the warrantless arrest of an accused is

later proven to be invalid, such fact is not

sufficient to cause to set aside a valid judgment

rendered upon sufficient complaint after trial

free from error.

Effect of admission to bail on objections to an

illegal arrest

1) Shall not bar the accused from challenging the

validity of the arrest or the legality of the

warrant issued, provided that he raises the

objection before he enters his plea.

2) the objection shall be resolved by the court as

early as practicable, but not later than the start

of the trial of the case.

Privilege from arrest

Under Section 11, Article VI of the 1987 constitution,

a senator or a member of the House of Representatives

shall, in all offenses punishable by not more than six

years imprisonment, be privileged from arrest when

the Congress is in session.

Does not apply

1) when not in session

2) When the offense is punishable more than

six years even if Congress is in session

Other exempt

Sovereigns and other Chiefs of State, ambassadors,

ministers plenipotentiary, ministers resident in charge

of the affairs are immune from the criminal jurisdiction

of the country of their assignment and are therefore

immune from arrest.

SEARCH AND SEIZURE

RULE 126

Section 1. Search warrant defined. — A search warrant

is an order in writing issued in the name of the

People of the Philippines, signed by a judge and

directed to a peace officer, commanding him to

search for personal property described therein and

bring it before the court.

Section 2. Court where application for search

warrant shall be filed. — An application for search

warrant shall be filed with the following:

a) Any court within whose territorial jurisdiction a

crime was committed.

b) For compelling reasons stated in the

application, any court within the judicial region

where the crime was committed if the place of the

commission of the crime is known, or any court

within the judicial region where the warrant shall be

enforced.

However, if the criminal action has already been

filed, the application shall only be made in the court

where the criminal action is pending.

Section 3. Personal property to be seized. — A

search warrant may be issued for the search and

seizure of personal property:

a) Subject of the offense;

b) Stolen or embezzled and other proceeds, or fruits

of the offense; or

c) Used or intended to be used as the means of

committing an offense.

Section 4. Requisites for issuing search warrant. —

A search warrant shall not issue except upon

probable cause in connection with one specific

offense to be determined personally by the judge

after examination under oath or affirmation of the

complainant and the witnesses he may produce, and

particularly describing the place to be searched and

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

the things to be seized which may be anywhere in

the Philippines.

Section 5. Examination of complainant; record. —

The judge must, before issuing the warrant,

personally examine in the form of searching

questions and answers, in writing and under oath,

the complainant and the witnesses he may produce

on facts personally known to them and attach to the

record their sworn statements, together with the

affidavits submitted.

Section 6. Issuance and form of search warrant. —

If the judge is satisfied of the existence of facts upon

which the application is based or that there is

probable cause to believe that they exist, he shall

issue the warrant, which must be substantially in the

form prescribed by these Rules.

Section 1. Search warrant defined. — A search warrant

is an order in writing issued in the name of the

People of the Philippines, signed by a judge and

directed to a peace officer, commanding him to

search for personal property described therein and

bring it before the court.

Nature of application for search warrant

It is a special criminal process and is heard ex parte. A

search warrant is not criminal action nor does it

represent a commencement of a criminal prosecution

even if it is entitled like a criminal action. It is not a

proceeding against a person but it is solely for the

discovery and to get possession of personal

property.

It is a special and peculiar remedy, drastic in nature, and

made necessary because of public necessity. It

resembles, in some respect, with what is commonly

known as John Doe proceedings.

John Doe proceedings - an independent investigatory

tool to ascertain whether a crime has been committed,

and if so, by whom. One aspect of a John Doe

proceeding is to allow law enforcement officers,

through a court order by a judge, to examine a witness

and to collect other sources of evidence to determine

whether there is criminal conduct which should be

prosecuted. It is similar because you can actually file

for a search warrant even before a criminal case is filed

in court. What it seeks to find out is whether or not

there is an evidence or there is cause to prosecute a

certain person for a criminal offense.

Rationale

Much like in warrants of arrest, the general rule is that

no search and seizure can be made without a valid

warrant issued by a competent judicial authority.

of the complainant and the witnesses,

together with the affidavit submitted

shall be attached to the record.

3) In the determination of probable cause, the

judge must examine, under oath or affirmation,

the complainant and such witnesses as the

4) The

warrant

issued

must

particularly

describe the place to be searched and persons

or things to be seized.

The long-standing rule is that a description of the place

to be searched is sufficient if the officer with the

warrant can with reasonable effort ascertain and

identify the place intended and distinguish it from

other places in the community. Any designation or

description that points out the place, to the

exclusion of all others, and on inquiry leads the

officers unerringly to it satisfies the constitutional

requirement.

5) The applicant and the witnesses must testify on

the facts, data or information personally

known to them.

Nullification of search warrant

1) The absence of any of these requisites will

cause the downright nullification of the search

warrant.

2) The issuance of a search warrant for more

than one offense would violate Section 4 of

Rule 126, and is not allowed.

3) Absent the element of personal knowledge

by the applicant or his witnesses, of the facts

upon which the issuance of a search warrant

may be justified, the warrant is not deemed

based on probable cause and is a nullity. Its

issuance being in legal contemplation, arbitrary.

Place must be particularly described

The caption of the search warrant provides or

indicates the address of petitioner as "Hernan

Cortez Street, Cebu City," while the body of the

search warrant states that that the address is

"Hernan Cortez Street, Mandaue City".

The Supreme Court did not consider the

discrepancy as sufficient to consider the warrant as

constitutionally infirm. It was not shown that

there was a street with the same name in Cebu

City, nor was it established that the officers

enforcing the warrant had difficulty locating the

premises of the petitioner which was actually in

Hernan Cortez Street, Mandaue City.

The Supreme Court said that the description of the

place to be searched is sufficient if the officer

with the warrant can, with reasonable effort,

ascertain and identify the place intended and

distinguish it from other places in the

community. Any designation or description known

to the locality that points out to the place to the

exclusion of all others and on inquiry leads the

officers unerringly to it satisfies the constitutional

requirement. (Uy v. BIR)

Things must be particularly described

A search warrant may be said to particularly describe

the things to be seized when:

1) the description therein is a specific as the

circumstances will ordinarily allow;

2) the description expresses a conclusion of fact

not of law, by which the warrant officer may be

guided in making the search and seizure;

3) the things described are limited to those who

bear a direct relation to the offense for which

the warrant is being issued.

The law does not require that the things to be seized,

must be described in precise and minute detail as to

leave no room for doubt on the part of the searching

authorities.

A search warrant is not sweeping authority

empowering a raiding party to undertake a fishing

expedition to seize and confiscate any and all kinds of

evidence or articles relating to a crime.

Contraband

When it pertains to contrabands or those things which

are illegal per se, there is less stringent requirements on

the jurisprudence as to the particular description.

When partly valid and partly void

As to the part where it is too general or it admits of

even those things which may not be in connection with

the crime or which may be connected with a valid

business therefore, the public officers or the officers

enforcing the search warrant actually had to apply

discretion. But as to the part where the things to be

seized or actually seized is actually particularly

described, the seizure of those things are valid.

Ownership

Ownership is of no consequence. It is sufficient that

the person against whom the warrant is directed has

control and possession of the properties sought to be

seized.

Section 5. Examination of complainant; record. — The

judge must, before issuing the warrant, personally

examine in the form of searching questions and

answers, in writing and under oath, the complainant

and the witnesses he may produce on facts

personally known to them and attach to the record

their sworn statements, together with the affidavits

submitted.

Section 6. Issuance and form of search warrant. — If the

judge is satisfied of the existence of facts upon which

the application is based or that there is probable

cause to believe that they exist, he shall issue the

warrant, which must be substantially in the form

prescribed by these Rules.

Form of search warrant

1) It must be in the name of the People of the

Philippines;

2) It must be signed by the judge after finding

probable cause;

3) The finding of probable cause must be through

the examination under oath or affirmation of

the complainant and the witnesses that he may

present, and must be personally made by the

judge through probing searching questions

4) Must particularly described the place to be

searched, or the person to be searched, and the

thing or things to be seized.

5) It must command a peace officer or a law

enforcement officer to search for personal

property described therein and bring it before

the court.

It has been consistently ruled that an accused is

estopped from assailing any irregularity of his arrest if

he fails to raise this issue or to move for the quashal of

the information against him on this ground before

arraignment. Any objection involving a warrant of

arrest or the procedure by which the court acquired

jurisdiction over the person of the accused must be

made before he enters his plea; otherwise, the

objection is deemed waived. (Rebellion v. People)

It bears stressing that the legality of the arrest affects

only the jurisdiction of the court over their persons.

Their warrantless arrests cannot, by themselves, be the

bases of their acquittal. (People v. Yau)

Section 7. Right to break door or window to effect search.

— The officer, if refused admittance to the place of

directed search after giving notice of his purpose

and authority, may break open any outer or inner

door or window of a house or any part of a house or

anything therein to execute the warrant or liberate

himself or any person lawfully aiding him when

unlawfully detained therein.

Principle of knock and announce

They may only break open any outer or inner door or

window of a house to execute the search warrant if

after said notice and demand such officers are refused

entry to the place of directed search. This is known as

the knock and announced principle which is embodied

in Anglo American law. The method of entry of an

officer into a dwelling in the presence or absence of

such notice are as important considerations in

assessing whether subsequent entry to the search

and/or arrest is constitutionally reasonable.

In case in which the occupants of the house being

searched refused to open the door despite the fact

that the searching party knocked on the door several

times and the agent saw the suspicious movements

of the people inside the house, such circumstances

will justify the searching party's forcible entry to the

house founded as it is on the apprehension that the

execution of their mission will be frustrated unless

they do so. (People v. Salangit)

Requisites

1) that the officer gives notice of his purpose

and authority;

2) he is refused admittance to the place of

directed search despite notice; and

3) the purpose of breaking is to execute the

warrant or to liberate himself or any person

lawfully aiding him when unlawfully detain

therein

Section 11. Receipt for the property seized. — The officer

Section 13. Search incident to lawful arrest. — A person

lawfully arrested may be searched for dangerous

without a search warrant.

Search incident to lawful arrest

The purpose of the rule is to protect the arresting

officer against physical harm from the person being

arrested, who might be armed with a concealed

weapon, and also to prevent the person arrested from

destroying the evidence within his reach.

Requisites

1) There must be a by valid arrest; and

2) The search must be limited to space and time.

 It is limited as to time when it is made

at the earliest possible opportunity

after the arrest and there must be no

considerable lapse of time.

 It is also limited as to space it is made

on the person arrested or the

immediate vicinity where he has

effective control, 1) to cart away

evidence or

2)to get weapon

Effect of noncompliance

1. If there is no valid arrest, then whatever is

searched incident to that arrest would be

fruits of the poisonous tree.

2. If there is a violation to the requirement that

the search must be limited to space and

time, all things searched which may violate the

limitation as to time or space will be

considered as fruits of the poisonous tree.

Consented search

It is when the right against warrantless searches has

been voluntarily waived. It occurs when a person gives

a law enforcement agent permission to search in areas

where such person has reasonable expectation of

privacy.

 Jurisprudence requires that in instances of

consented searches, it is fundamental that, to

constitute a waiver: the right to waive exists.

 The person involved has knowledge of the

existence of such right.

 The said person had an actual intention to

relinquish such right

The implied agreement to a search, if there was any,

could not have been more than mere passive

conformity given under intimidating or coercive

circumstances, and is thus considered no consent

at all within the purview of the constitutional

guarantee.

Customs search

It could be in a wharf, in a port, i.e. airport or seaport.

It could be in vessels or aircrafts so long as it is

pursuant to the tariff and customs codes.

What is common in the implementation of these laws

is that the police or enforcement officer has the initial

right to ask any person who may be carrying things,

which they reasonably believe would be under or

covered by these respective laws to ask for the

authority to transport it or the authority to have it in

their possession.

In the absence of any papers, then they will have

already reasonable justification and or probable cause

to conduct a further search or inspection

Routine checks

1) Routine checks in airports

2) Routine checks in seaports

3) Public transport terminals

4) Jail safety

In these public areas, there is a diminished expectation

of privacy; because inspections are conducted in these

public areas for the safety of the general public. The

Supreme Court has continuously upheld that the

limited intrusion into the person and the things that

they may bring into these public spaces is a valid

warrantless search.

Related laws

1) Airports - Republic Act 6235

2) Seaport - Executive Order Number 513

Plain view doctrine

The doctrine states that the objects within the sight of

an officer who has a right to be in a position to have

the view, are subject to seizure and may be presented

as evidence.

Elements

1) A prior valid intrusion based on the valid

warrantless arrest in which the police are legally

present in the pursuit of their official duties

2) The evidence was inadvertently discovered

by the police who have the right to be where

they are.

3) The evidence must be immediately apparent

4) Plain view justified where seizure of evidence

without further search

Stop and frisk/ Terry search

Two purposes

1. The general interests of effective crime

prevention and detection; and

2. The safety of the police officer to take steps

to assure himself that the person with whom

he deals is not armed with a deadly weapon that

could be used against him.

Two parts

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

1) Stop - a valid stop by an officer requires that he

has a reasonable and articulable belief that a

criminal activity has happened or is about to

happen. This is based on the experience of the

law enforcement officer

2) Frisk - the frisk must be merely a pat down

outside the person's outer garment, and not

unreasonably intrusive.

Extensive search

If upon you frisking on the outside garment, there is

reasonable belief that there is a concealed weapon, then

that will allow or authorize the law enforcement officer

to do a more extensive search of the body of the

person.

Search of moving vehicle

To do a valid stop of the moving vehicle, there must

be an initial determination of probable cause which in

this instance means or signifies a reasonable ground of

suspicion, supported by circumstances, which are

sufficiently strong in themselves to warrant a cautious

man's belief that an offense has been committed, and

that the items articles or objects sought in connection

with said offense are subject to seizure and destruction

by law is in the place to be searched.

Normally permissible searches of moving vehicle

1) where the officer merely draws aside the

curtain of a vacant vehicle which is parked on

the public fairgrounds;

2) simply looks into a vehicle - flashes a light

therein without opening the cars door;

3) where the occupants are not subjected to a

physical or body search;

4) where the inspection of the vehicle is limited to

a visual search or visual inspection; and

5) where the routine check is conducted in a fixed

area.

Extensive search

If after conducting the visual search, there is cause to

do a more extensive search, then that would be

allowed.

Requirements for a valid checkpoint

1) the location of checkpoints must be fixed;

2) the

location

of

Aerial target zoning

Search of a particular area. If there is no priorly

Exigent and emergency circumstances

This exception applies during extraordinary times

wherein warrantless searches are allowed, such as coup

d'état and rebellions, where the courts are not open.

This could also apply during times of unrest or when

there is general political instability. Where because of

the exigencies of what is happening in the country, a

valid warrantless search may be conducted to aid in the

administration of justice.

Inspection of buildings and other premises to enforce

building laws, fire laws, safety standards laws

In the Building Code of the Philippines, building

officials has authority to inspect compliance with the

Building Code as to the structure, the materials that

were used, compliance with a minimum requirement as

to height, etc. For the purpose of this inspection, there

is no need to secure a prior judicial search warrant.

In the inspection of the Bureau of Fire officials for

compliance with the Fire Code - whether there is

enough fire exits, enough fire extinguishers, or other

safety protocols that are required under the Fire Code

- no need for prior search warrant for the inspection.

This also applies to our Sanitation Code of the

Philippines - to ensure that there is compliance with

this, the officers in charge with implementing the

Sanitation Code does not need any prior search warrant

for the conduct of inspection to see to it that there is

compliance with the Code.

Doctrine of the fruit of the poisonous tree

Section 3(2), Article III of the 1987 Constitution An

exclusionary rule which instructs that the evidence

obtained and confiscated on the occasion of such

unreasonable searches and seizures are deemed

tainted and should be excluded for being the

proverbial fruit of a poisonous tree.

Any evidence obtained in violation of such

constitutional provision shall be inadmissible for any

purpose in any proceeding. The evidence obtained

through an unlawful search would be inadmissible as

evidence against the accused, and this applies to both

instances of illegally obtained search warrant or invalid

warrantless search.

Effect of waiver of the illegal warrantless arrest

The inadmissibility of the fruit of the poisonous tree is

not waived, even if objecting to the validity of the

warrant of arrest or search warrant is already

deemed waived, because it was not a questioned

before the entry of the plea.

Civil damages and criminal liability

Rule 126 of the Rules on Criminal Procedure No

1) The proceedings under Rule 126 of the Rules

on the Revised Rules on Criminal Procedure

do not provide for the filing of the counter

2) the aggrieved party have the right to seek

Code.

3) This liability shall be separate and distinct from

any criminal liability that may arise from the

129 of the RPC, or possibly searching domicile

without witnesses under Article 130 of the

RPC.

Relating to the Constitutional right

1) The provision of Section 2, Article III of the

government

Section 14. Motion to quash a search warrant or to

suppress evidence; where to file. — A motion to quash a

search warrant and/or to suppress evidence

obtained thereby may be filed in and acted upon

only by the court where the action has been

instituted. If no criminal action has been

instituted, the motion may be filed in and

resolved by the court that issued the search

warrant. However, if such court failed to resolve the

motion and a criminal case is subsequent filed in

another court, the motion shall be resolved by the

latter court.

1) If there is still no criminal complaint or

information filed in court and then you filed an

application for a search warrant and then a

search warrant is subsequently issued, the

motion may be filed in and resolved by the

court that issued the search warrant.

2) A motion to quash a search warrant and/or to

suppress evidence obtained thereby may be

filed in and acted upon only by the court

where the action has been instituted

3) If such court failed to resolve the motion and

a criminal case is subsequent filed in another

court, the motion shall be resolved by the

latter court

Who may assail the issuance of a search warrant?

Well settled is the rule that the legality of seizure can

be contested only by the party whose right has been

impaired thereby and the objection to an unlawful

search and seizure is purely personal and cannot be

availed of by any third party.

If the proper party in interest, the person who is

actually prejudiced by the illegal search, wants to file

for a motion to quash, or motion to suppress evidence,

there is no need for the public prosecutor's conformity

with that motion.

The question of whether there was abuse in the

enforcement of the challenged search warrant is not

within the scope of the motion to quash or the motion

to suppress evidence. Otherwise stated, the manner of

serving the warrant and effecting the search are

not an issue to be resolved in a motion to quash.

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

The remedies against such abuse are penal, civil, or

administrative.

Remedies

1) The motion to quash the search warrant; -

whether or not there is a case filed in court

2) The motion to suppress evidence obtained by

virtue of the invalid warrant; - when there is no

case filed in court, before the accused enter his

plea

3) Objection to the admissibility of the evidence

obtained by virtue of an invalid warrant when

such evidence is offered in evidence - when the

trial is already ongoing when the party has

already presented the things seized under an

illegal search warrant

A search warrant as an incident of a criminal case filed

Where the criminal case of which the search warrant is

an incident has already been filed before the trial court

for the purpose of determining the proper remedy

from a grant or denial of a motion to quash a search

warrant, where the search warrant is issued as an

incident in a pending criminal case, the quashal of a

search warrant is merely interlocutory. There is still

something more to be done in the said criminal case

and the determination of the guilt of the accused

therein is yet to be determined.

Since you have no other remedy but to wait for the

entire case to be finished before you can question

whether the grant or the denial of the search warrant is

valid or not, then you can raise it up to a higher court,

to the Court of Appeals via petition for certiorari

under Rule 65 on the grounds of grave abuse of

discretion.

A search warrant in anticipation of a criminal case

The denial or the grant of the search warrant actually

disposes of the case.

RIGHT TO BAIL

Article III, 1987 Constitution

SECTION 13. All persons, except those charged

with offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua when

evidence of guilt is strong, shall, before conviction,

be bailable by sufficient sureties, or be released on

recognizance as may be provided by law. The right

to bail shall not be impaired even when the privilege

of the writ of habeas corpus is suspended. Excessive

bail shall not be required.

Bail

A security given for the release of a person in

custody of the law, furnished by him or a bondsman,

to guarantee his appearance before any court as

required under the conditions hereinafter specified.

(Sec 1, Rule 114)

Section 1. Bail defined. — Bail is a security given for

the release of the person in custody of the law,

furnished by him or a bondsman to guarantee his

appearance before any court as required under the

conditions herein after specified. Bail may be given

in the form of corporate surety property, bond, cash

deposit, or recognizance.

Characteristics

1) Bail is a security - the purpose of the giving of

bail is to guarantee the appearance of the

accused at the trial.

2) Bail is furnished by the person to be released

or bondsman

3) The security is given to guarantee the

appearance of the person released before any

court as required under the conditions

specified under Rule 114.

Elements

1) The right is a constitutional right

Constitution lays down the following fundamental

tenets on bail;

 All persons charged before their conviction for

a criminal offense shall be entitled to bail. This

is the general rule.

 The suspension of the privilege of the writ of

habeas corpus does not impair the right to bail.

 Excessive bail is not required.

Purpose of bail

1) To relieve an accused from imprisonment until

his conviction and yet assure appearance at the

trial and at the same time enable him to prepare

his

defense

without

being

subject

to

punishment prior to conviction.

2) To prevent the release of an accused who

might otherwise be dangerous to society or

whom judges might not want to be released.

3) It

acts

as

reconciling

mechanism

to

accommodate both the accused's interest in

liberty before trial and society's interest in

assuring accused presence at the trial.

4) The right to bail is granted because in all

criminal prosecutions the accused is presumed

innocent, that without bail bond the accused

under detention cannot be released.

General rules on bail

1. All persons charged before their conviction

for a criminal offense shall be entitled to bail.

2. The suspension of the privilege of the writ

of habeas corpus does not impair the right

to bail.

3. Excessive bail is not required.

4. The right can be invoked or is available the

moment there is an arrest, with or without a

warrant

5. The person to be released must be in custody

of the law.

6. Before or after information is filed

7. The hearing must be necessary and summary

Narciso v. Sta Romana Cruz

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

The following are the duties of the trial judge in a

petition for bail in the offenses as mentioned:

a) Notify the prosecutor of the hearing of the

application for bail or require him to submit his

recommendation (Section 18, Rule 114 of the Rules of

Court as amended;

b) Conduct a hearing of the application for bail

regardless of whether or not the prosecution refuses to

present evidence to show that the guilt of the accused

is strong for the purpose of enabling the court to

exercise its sound discretion (Sections 7 and 8, supra);

c) Decide whether the evidence of guilt of the

accused is strong based on the summary of evidence

of the prosecution (Baylon v. Sison, supra);

d) If the guilt of the accused is not strong, discharge

the accused upon the approval of the bail bond.

(Section 19, supra). Otherwise, petition should be

denied.

The form of bail is the choice of the accused

1) Corporate surety – Bonding company

the accused and an officer of the

corporate surety (solidarily liable)

2) Property bond - If the accused has no cash

Section 11. Property bond, how posted. — A

Section 12. Qualifications of sureties in property

bond. — The qualification of sureties in a

(a) Each must be a resident owner of real

(b) Where there is only one surety, his real

In all cases, every surety must be worth the

Section 23. Arrest of accused out on bail. — For the

purpose of surrendering the accused, the bondsmen

may arrest him or, upon written authority endorsed

on a certified copy of the undertaking, cause him to

be arrested by a police officer or any other person of

suitable age and discretion.

An accused released on bail may be re-arrested

without the necessity of a warrant if he attempts to

depart from the Philippines without permission of

the court where the case is pending.

Constitutional restrictions

Right to travel

The constitutional right to travel of a person accused

of a crime and is undergoing criminal prosecution is

limited by the bail that he is on.

If the accused wants to travel abroad, he must ask leave

of court or permission from the court for that travel.

There must be a justification for the necessity of the

travel abroad.

Right to liberty of abode

When the accused chooses to transfer his residency, he

is duty bound to inform the court of the same. In that

sense, the right of the accused to liberty of abode is also

limited.

Person to be released must be in custody of the law

Custody of the law may be attained when:

a) An accused is validly arrested;

b) He submits to the jurisdiction of the court

upon his appearance before the court;

c) There is constructive custody when there are

reasons that he cannot appear before the court

to apply for bail, but he still accedes to the

court's jurisdiction and that his custody is

already considered custody in law.

The right to bail then may only be availed of by a

person in the custody of the law or otherwise deprived

of his liberty. Since bail is obtained for the provisional

liberty of the accused, the same cannot be authorized

or posted before custody of the accused has been

acquired by judicial authority either by his arrest, with

or without warrant, or his voluntary surrender.

The concept of custody under the law does not merely

signify restraint over the person or custody over the

body of the accused. It is not limited to detention. It

may also be present when the accused knows that his

liberty is already limited and that he submits to the

limitation on his liberty.

The rationale for this rule is to discourage the practice

where the accused could just send another on his

behalf to post his bail without recognizing the

jurisdiction of the court.

A waiver of defense of lack of jurisdiction

The mere application for bail constitutes a waiver of

the defense of lack of jurisdiction over the person

of the accused. This is because upon application for

bail, affirmative relief is sought, thus, one is

considered to have voluntarily appeared before the

court

Constructive custody

One important concept that we reiterate when we talk

about custody of the law is- if the person of the accused

is in the hospital, but only instances where there is

impossibility for the person in the hospital to come to

the court to ask for or apply for bail, but he submits to

the jurisdiction of the court - that is considered

constructive custody under the law. Therefore, the

accused can already apply for bail.

Application of bail

The Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure on Bail

pertains to criminal actions because it is under the

Rules of Court. The Constitution, as interpreted in

many cases, does not only pertain to criminal

prosecutions. All persons except those charged with

offenses punishable by Reclusion Perpetua when

evidence of guilt is strong shall be, for conviction, be

bailable by sufficient sureties or be released on

recognizance as may be provided for by law. The right

to bail shall not be impaired even when the privilege of

the writ of habeas corpus is suspended and excessive

bail shall not be required.

The Constitution is silent as to whether or not it only

applies to criminal prosecution. The interpretation of

the Supreme Court, however, is that it may apply to

other situations when there is a deprivation of liberty

or when a person is under the custody of the law but

not necessarily in the context of criminal proceedings.

EXCEPTIONS TO RIGHT TO BAIL

The right to bail in relation to military men who

are charged for offenses and the right to bail in

relation to extradition cases

As to the military, the right to bail has traditionally not

been recognized and is not available as an exception to

the provision of the Constitution on the right to bail.

The right to a speedy trial is given more emphasis in a

military setting but the right to bail does not exist. The

unique structure of the military should be enough

reason to exempt military men from the constitutional

coverage of the right to bail.

The argument that denial for the military of the right

to bail would violate the equal protection clause is not

acceptable because military personnel are a class of

their own, they are not the same as civilians.

They are governed by a different code of conduct,

organization and set of rules and when they are

prosecuted, based on the articles of war and based on

the rules under the military, the right to bail is not

available to them because usually the violations are

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

considered violations against the commander in

chief and violations of this nature go very much into

the stability of the military hierarchy.

GR: the right to bail in the military is only not given

for military offenses in Military Court Martials

XPN: when the military is involved in a criminal

action, which is filed in the prosecutor's office and then

filed in the regular courts, then in that instance, they

are allowed to avail of their constitutional right to bail.

Extradition proceedings

This is when a person, whether or not he is a citizen of

the Philippines, has a criminal case or a case in a

jurisdiction that is not the Philippines and where the

Philippines and that particular foreign nation have an

extradition treaty and because of the treaty, the

Philippines as a party to the treaty is mandated to take

custody of the person to be extradited.

The Government of the United States of

America v. Purganan

Extradition proceedings

The Supreme Court held that the constitutional

provision on bail does not apply to extradition

proceedings. It is available only in criminal

proceedings.

In extradition proceedings, prospective extraditees

are generally not entitled to notice and hearing

before warrants for their arrest can be issued.

Neither are they entitled to the right to bail and

provisional

liberty

while

the

extradition

proceedings are pending.

The policy is that a prospective extraditee is arrested

and detained, to avoid his flight from justice. On the

extraditee lies the burden of showing that he will not

flee once bail is granted.

The extradition court is that called upon to ascertain

the guilt or the innocence of the person sought to be

extradited. The ultimate purpose of extradition

proceedings in court is only to determine whether

the extradition request complies with the

extradition treaty applicable, and whether the

person sought is extraditable.

Exception

Accordingly and to best serve the ends of justice, we

believe and so hold that, after a potential extraditee

has been arrested or placed under the custody of the

law, bail may be applied for and granted as an

exception, only upon a clear and convincing

evidence showing

1) that, once granted bail, the applicant will

not be a flight risk or a danger to the

community; and

2) that there exist special, humanitarian

and

compelling

circumstances

including, as a matter of reciprocity,

those cited by the highest court in the

requesting state when it grants provisional

liberty in extradition cases therein.

xxx First, we note that the exercise of the State's

power to deprive an individual of his liberty is not

necessarily

limited

to

criminal

proceedings.

Respondents in administrative proceedings,

such as deportation and quarantine, have

likewise been detained. Second, to limit bail to

criminal proceedings would be to close our eyes

to our jurisprudential history.

Government of Hong Kong Special

Administrative Region v. Olalia Jr.

In a subsequent ruling in the case of Government of

Hong Kong Special Administrative Region vs. Olalia Jr.

somehow abandoned the ruling in the case of

Purganan. The Supreme Court ruled that following

the trends in international law;

1) The

growing

importance

of

the

individual person in public international

law, who, in the 20th century has gradually

attained global recognition.

2) The higher value now being given to

human rights in the international sphere.

3) The corresponding duty of the countries to

observe this universal human rights in

fulfilling their treaty obligation. And;

4) The duty of the Supreme Court to balance

the rights of the individual under our

fundamental law on one hand, in the law

on extradition on the other.

Extradition proceeding being sui generis

The standard of proof required in granting or

denying bail can neither be the proof beyond

reasonable doubt in criminal cases nor the

standard of proof of preponderance of evidence

in civil cases. While administrative in character, the

standard

of

substantial

evidence

used

in

administrative cases cannot likewise apply given

the object of extradition law which is to prevent the

prospective extraditee from fleeing our jurisdiction.

In his Separate Opinion in Purganan, then Associate

Justice, now Chief Justice Reynato S. Puno,

proposed that a new standard which he termed

"clear and convincing evidence" should be used

in granting bail in extradition cases. According to

him, this standard should be lower than proof

beyond

reasonable

doubt

but

higher

than

preponderance of evidence. The potential extraditee

must prove by "clear and convincing evidence"

that he is not a flight risk and will abide with all

the orders and processes of the extradition

court.

Bail hearings are mandatory

Bail hearing is necessary even if the prosecution does

not interpose any objection or leaves the application

for bail to the sound discretion of the court. A

hearing is required in order for the court to ascertain

the adequacy of the amount of bail under the

guidelines set forth in section 9 rule 114 of the rules

of criminal procedure.

Further, failure to conduct a hearing when

required before fixing bail will violate due process

and disregard of the established rule of law by

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

depriving the prosecution of the opportunity to

prove that the evidence of guilt against the

accused is strong and will constitute gross

ignorance of the law or incompetence which will

subject the judge to disciplinary action.

Ignorance of this type, cannot be excused by a claim

of good faith or excusable negligence. Thus, it is still

mandatory for the court to conduct a hearing and

ask searching and clarificatory questions for the

purpose of determining the existence of strong

evidence against the accused although the

prosecution interposed no objection to the grant of

bail or refuse to adduce evidence that the guilt of the

accused was strong.

In reexamining Purganan the Court made the following

observation:

1) The exercise of the state's power to deprive an

individual of his liberty is not necessarily

limited

to

criminal

proceedings,

respondents in administrative proceedings,

such as deportation and quarantine have

likewise been detained.

2) To limit bail to criminal proceedings would

be to close our eyes to jurisprudential

history. The Philippine jurisprudence has not

limited the exercise of the right to bail to

criminal proceedings only. This court has

admitted to bail persons who are not involved

in criminal proceedings. In fact, bail has been

allowed in jurisdictions to persons in

detention

during

the

pendency

of

administrative proceedings, taking into

cognizance the obligation of the Philippines on

their international convention to uphold

human rights.

Section 3. No release or transfer except on court

order or bail. – No person under detention by legal

process shall be released or transferred except upon

order of the court or when he is admitted to bail.

5) Recognizance (Rules of Court, Rule 114,

Sec 1) – an obligation of record entered into

authorized to take it with a condition to do

A simple personal obligation or undertaking

Section 15. Recognizance. — Whenever allowed by

law or these Rules, the court may release a person in

custody to his own recognizance or that of a

responsible person. (15a)

A person may be released on recognizance in the

following cases:

1) When the offense charge is for violation of

not exceed six months imprisonment and or

a P2000 fine.

2) When a person has been in custody for a

3) When the accused has applied for probation

pending the resolution of the case, but no

Probation is a disposition under which a defendant,

after conviction and sentence, is released subject to a

condition imposed by the court and under the

supervision of a probation officer.

4) In case of a youthful offender, held for

physical and mental examination, trial, or

appeal, he is unable to furnish bail and under

circumstances envisaged by PD 603, as

amended

Section 24. Release of Children on Recognizance to

the Parents, Guardian, Custodian or Nearest

Relative — The release of a child from custody

during the pendency of the case involving an offense

not punishable by death, reclusion perpetua or life

imprisonment may be ordered by the court only

after a hearing for that purpose, and upon favorable

recommendation of the social worker assigned to

the child with due notice to the public prosecutor,

the Sanggunian where the accused resides, and the

private complainant. The child shall be released to

the custody of a willing and responsible mother or

father, or appropriate guardian or custodian, or in

their absence, the nearest relative, who shall be

responsible for the child's good behavior and

appearance in court whenever required.

No child shall be ordered detained in jail pending

trial or hearing of the child's case.

Department of Social Welfare and Development,

which

shall

ensure

the

implementation

of

In the absence of a "Bahay Pag-asa" established by

Section 26. Bail as a Matter of right. — For purposes

of bail, the privileged mitigating circumstance of

minority shall be considered.

In all cases the giving or posting of a bail bond by

the accused is tantamount to the submission of his

person to the jurisdiction of the Court.

Who may invoke?

1) Arrested

2) Detained

3) Deprived of their liberty whether or not an

information or a criminal complaint has been

filed

GR: All those who are already in custody of law may

avail of the right to bail as a matter of right

XPN: Those charged with offenses punishable with

reclusion perpetua, when evidence of guilt is strong

Bail may either be:

1) A matter of right

2) A matter of discretion

A MATTER OF RIGHT OR DISCRETION

Section 4. Bail, a matter of right; exception. — All

persons in custody shall be admitted to bail as a

matter of right, with sufficient sureties, or released

on recognize as prescribed by law or this Rule (a)

before or after conviction by the Metropolitan

Trial Court, Municipal Trial Court, Municipal

Trial Court in Cities, or Municipal Circuit Trial

Court, and (b) before conviction by the Regional

Trial Court of an offense not punishable by

death, reclusion perpetua, or life imprisonment.

(4a)

Section 5. Bail, when discretionary. — Upon

conviction by the Regional Trial Court of an

offense not punishable by death, reclusion

perpetua, or life imprisonment, admission to bail

is discretionary. The application for bail may be

filed and acted upon by the trial court despite the

filing of a notice of appeal, provided it has not

transmitted the original record to the appellate court.

However, if the decision of the trial court

convicting the accused changed the nature of

the offense from non-bailable to bailable, the

application for bail can only be filed with and

resolved by the appellate court.

Should the court grant the application, the accused

may be allowed to continue on provisional liberty

during the pendency of the appeal under the same

bail subject to the consent of the bondsman.

If the penalty imposed by the trial court is

imprisonment exceeding six (6) years, the

accused shall be denied bail, or his bail shall be

cancelled upon a showing by the prosecution,

with notice to the accused, of the following or

other similar circumstances:

(a) That he is a recidivist, quasi-recidivist, or

habitual delinquent, or has committed the crime

aggravated by the circumstance of reiteration;

(b) That he has previously escaped from legal

confinement, evaded sentence, or violated the

conditions of his bail without valid justification;

(c) That he committed the offense while under

probation, parole, or conditional pardon;

(d) That the circumstances of his case indicate the

probability of flight if released on bail; or

(e) That there is undue risk that he may commit

another crime during the pendency of the appeal.

The appellate court may, motu proprio or on

motion of any party, review the resolution of the

Regional Trial Court after notice to the adverse party

in either case. (5a)

When is bail a matter of right?

1) Before or after conviction by the Metropolitan

Trial Court, or first level courts, or while on

appeal.

2) Before conviction by a Regional Trial Court

except if the offense charged is punishable by

reclusion perpetua, life imprisonment or death,

where the evidence of guilt is strong.

3) Before conviction by a Regional trial court for

death, life imprisonment or reclusion perpetua,

when the evidence of guilt is not strong.

Remedy

1) The remedy is a petition for certiorari under

Rule 65 because the court committed grave

abuse of discretion amounting to excess or lack

of jurisdiction for issuing the denial of the bail

when bail is a matter of right.

2) Mandamus may also at the same time be

availed to compel know the grant of bail, which

is a matter of right When bail is a matter of

right, the court is left with no discretion but to

grant the same.

Criminal Procedure | VENTEROSO

Hearing is always required whether it's a matter of

right or a matter of discretion.

When is bail a matter of discretion?

1) After conviction by the RTC, if the penalty

imposed is 6 years or lower

2) After conviction for an offense which is

punishable with six (6) years and one (1) day

to twenty (20) years, if the following

circumstances are not present:

a) The accused is a recidivist, quasi-

recidivist or a habitual delinquent or has

committed the crime aggravated by the

circumstance of reiteracion.

b) The accused is found to have previously

escaped from legal confinement, evaded

sentence or has violated the conditions of

his bail without valid justification.

c) The accused committed the offense while

on probation, parole or under conditional

pardon.

d) The circumstance of the accused or his case

indicate the probability of flight, if released

on bail.

e) There is an undue risk that during the

pendency of the appeal, the accused may

commit another crime.

Where to appeal bail? (Sec 5)

1) When there is already a notice of appeal but the

entire record of the case has not yet been

transmitted to the appellate court – RTC

2) When there is already a notice of appeal and

the entire record has already been transmitted
